blocks.html: Boundaries questions test one thing: the punctuation that joins, separates, or interrupts clauses. Every answer choice keeps the same words and changes only the marks — so the whole question lives at one seam in the sentence.

blocks.title: The boundary rule
text: Find the seam — the spot where the answer choices differ — and test each side of it alone. If [u]both[/u] sides can stand alone as complete sentences (independent clauses), you must use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
If either side cannot stand alone, those three strong joints are all wrong — you need a comma or nothing at all.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a legal colon
blocks.intro: The SAT's favorite boundary trap is the colon. Read how each part of this sentence earns its punctuation:

segments.text: The reef survey produced a surprising result
coral cover had increased in every protected zone

markers.label: A complete sentence — subject (survey) plus verb (produced). The colon is legal only because this half could end with a period.
The colon acts as a gate: it promises that what follows will name or explain the "surprising result."
The payoff. After a legal colon, anything may follow — a list, a phrase, or, as here, another complete sentence.

blocks.note: Test a colon by covering everything after it. If what remains is not a sentence you could end with a period, the colon is wrong — no matter how natural it sounds.

wrong.text: The survey measured: coral cover, fish density, and water clarity.
wrong.why: "The survey measured" is not a complete sentence — the verb is left hanging without its object. A colon can never interrupt a clause that is still in progress.

correct.text: The survey measured three variables: coral cover, fish density, and water clarity.
correct.why: "The survey measured three variables" stands alone as a complete sentence, so the colon legally introduces the list that names those variables.

blocks.title: Semicolon = period in disguise
blocks.text: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, exactly like a period does. If you could not put a period at the seam, you cannot put a semicolon there either. A comma alone between two independent clauses is always wrong — that error is called a comma splice, and the SAT plants it in the choices on nearly every boundaries question.

wrong.text: The zone was protected in 2019, coral cover rose within two seasons.
wrong.why: Both halves are independent clauses, and a comma alone cannot join them — this is a comma splice. To keep the comma, you would need a FANBOYS word after it (", and coral cover rose").

correct.text: The zone was protected in 2019; coral cover rose within two seasons.
correct.why: The semicolon is a legal joint between two related independent clauses — each side could stand alone as its own sentence.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.intro: Marine biologist Ana Ruiz spent a decade mapping the reef's recovery ______ her data now guides marine-park policy in three countries.  (A) recovery, her  (B) recovery her  (C) recovery, and, her  (D) recovery; her

steps.label: Find the seam
steps.content: The choices differ only at the boundary between "recovery" and "her data." Same words, different marks — this is a boundaries question, so ignore meaning and test the clauses.

steps.label: Test the left side
steps.content: "Marine biologist Ana Ruiz spent a decade mapping the reef's recovery" has a subject (Ana Ruiz) and a main verb (spent). It could end with a period — independent clause.

steps.label: Test the right side
steps.content: "Her data now guides marine-park policy in three countries" also has a subject (data) and a verb (guides) — a second independent clause.

steps.label: Apply the rule, eliminate
steps.content: IC + IC needs a period, a semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS. (A) is a comma splice. (B) fuses the clauses with nothing at all — a run-on. (C) buries "and" between two commas, which joins nothing.
steps.note: Notice that every wrong choice fails the same one rule — you never had to weigh style or tone.

steps.label: Answer: (D) recovery; her
steps.content: The semicolon is the only legal joint offered between the two independent clauses.

items: Choices that keep the words and change only the punctuation mean one thing: test the seam, not the meaning.
Period, semicolon, and comma + FANBOYS are interchangeable joints — all three require an independent clause on [u]both[/u] sides.
A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice. It is never correct on the SAT.
A colon must follow a complete sentence; what follows the colon can be anything — list, phrase, or full clause.
Interrupters need matching punctuation on both sides: two commas or two dashes, never one of each.
